title: JVM Internals, Memory & Practical Tuning
goal: Understand how Java executes, diagnose memory and concurrency failures, and tune backend workloads using reproducible evidence.
outcomes: Trace source, bytecode, class loading, frames and optimized execution.
Explain heap versus stack without confusing primitive values, references and object fields.
Distinguish allocation pressure, retained leaks, native memory, stack exhaustion and OS termination.
Use GC logs, thread dumps, JFR and native-memory tracking to investigate a bounded workload.
Defend a memory budget and a single-variable tuning decision with correctness, latency and resource evidence.
studyGuidance: Suggested pace: four to six weeks; prioritize memory areas, references, reachability and diagnostics before tuning.

Foundational lessons can be studied after Java Core; the operational investigation is best done after Production Thinking. Module completion prerequisites apply to the recommended sequence, not access to the lessons.
Use Java 25 documentation as the reference and record your actual JDK vendor, version, architecture and collector. Adjust commands to that version.
Separate JVM specification guarantees from HotSpot implementation details and measurements on your machine.
Use plain Java and local disposable processes. Set workload and time bounds; never trigger host-level exhaustion to prove a point.
Record Prediction, Runtime settings, Observation, Explanation, Uncertainty and Next experiment in existing notes.
Treat dumps and recordings as potentially sensitive; use synthetic data, limited durations and a cleanup policy.
Ask AI for one hint or an evidence review, then explain the conclusion without notes.
completionCriteria: Explain all core runtime and memory areas with a request diagram, including aliases and primitive fields.
Finish the eight labs with runnable checks, bounded experiments and evidence-backed explanations.
Diagnose the worker capstone, correct a root cause and evaluate one justified runtime change.
Explain concurrency guarantees, measurement limitations and rollback thresholds without notes.

material.explanation: The JDK supplies development and diagnostic tools; the JVM executes class files. HotSpot is one JVM implementation. javac translates source into bytecode, not necessarily the final machine instructions executed by the CPU. A running VM loads classes, manages memory and threads, and can interpret or compile methods. JVM specification concepts describe an abstract machine; actual layouts and optimizations depend on the implementation and version.

workedExample.scenario: A plain Java Main prints a calculated total.
steps: Compile Main.java into Main.class and identify the entry point.
The VM loads required classes and executes main
frequently executed code may later be compiled.

commonMistakes: One Java statement is not necessarily one bytecode or one CPU instruction.
guidedExercise: Run java -version and javac -version
record vendor, version and architecture.
Compile and run a small program and sketch the source → class file → VM → CPU path.
material.independentExercise: Explain how the same class file can run on different operating systems and what native code changes that claim.
recallQuestions: What does javac produce?
Which responsibilities belong to HotSpot rather than the Java language?

acceptanceCriteria: Distinguish source, bytecode and native instructions.
Identify the exact JDK used in the lab.

topics.title: Class loading, linking and initialization
topics.description: Loading obtains a class representation.
learningGoals: Explain the observed initializer order.
Separate loading, linking and initialization.
examples: A service references Config and invokes a static method.

tasks.title: Record a prediction and runtime assumptions

Explain a backend failure or design tradeoff

material.explanation: Loading obtains a class representation. Linking verifies bytecode, prepares class storage, and resolves symbolic references, with resolution allowed to be lazy. Initialization executes static initializers at defined active-use points. A class identity includes its defining loader as well as its name, so two loaders can define distinct classes with the same name. Initialization has synchronization rules and can fail; static initialization is not simply performed whenever source mentions a class.

workedExample.scenario: A service references Config and invokes a static method.
steps: Predict which operation first initializes Config
a compile-time constant can behave differently.
Print from static initializers and compare the actual order with the prediction.

commonMistakes: Loading a class and initializing it are different events.
guidedExercise: Create two classes with static initialization messages.
Compare accessing a compile-time constant, creating an instance and calling a static method.
material.independentExercise: Explain a failed static initializer and distinguish ClassNotFoundException from NoClassDefFoundError using a tiny example.
recallQuestions: Why does the defining loader affect identity?
When can initialization be triggered?

acceptanceCriteria: Explain the observed initializer order.
Separate loading, linking and initialization.

topics.description: Each JVM frame has local variables and an operand stack.
learningGoals: Trace one method instruction by instruction.

material.explanation: Each JVM frame has local variables and an operand stack. Bytecode loads values, performs operations, invokes methods and returns results. This operand stack is an execution model, distinct from the collection type Stack and from a full operating-system thread stack. Disassembly connects source to runtime behavior, but HotSpot can transform execution substantially after compilation, so bytecode alone cannot establish real performance.

workedExample.scenario: static int add(int a, int b) returns a + b.
steps: Use javap -c -p Main and identify iload, iadd and ireturn.
Trace the operands pushed and consumed, then compare a method invocation.

commonMistakes: Bytecode instruction counts do not directly predict CPU time.
guidedExercise: Compile an addition method and a method that calls it.
Annotate local-variable indexes and operand-stack changes.
material.independentExercise: Disassemble a loop with a null check and explain its branches without guessing its optimized machine code.
recallQuestions: How do locals differ from operands?
Why can JIT execution differ from the disassembly?

acceptanceCriteria: Trace one method instruction by instruction.
Explain a method call and return.

topics.description: The heap conceptually holds objects and arrays and is shared across threads.
learningGoals: Locate reference locals and object fields correctly.

material.explanation: The heap conceptually holds objects and arrays and is shared across threads. JVM stacks hold per-thread method frames; each frame contains local variables, operands and method bookkeeping. HotSpot also consumes native memory for class metadata, compiled code, thread stacks and other subsystems. A primitive field can be inside a heap object, while a stack local can hold a reference. These categories describe roles, not a portable promise that every source variable occupies a particular physical address.

workedExample.scenario: A request method has int retries and a reference to an Order with an int amount field.
steps: Draw the frame local values and the referenced object, including amount inside the object.
Add metadata, compiled code and thread resources outside the heap budget.

commonMistakes: Primitives always live on the stack, and -Xmx limits the entire process, are both incorrect.
guidedExercise: Draw the memory map of a request handler.
Label which regions are shared and which are associated with a thread.
material.independentExercise: Explain why a process can exceed its maximum heap while heap usage remains stable.
recallQuestions: Where can a primitive field live?
Which memory is not included in -Xmx?

acceptanceCriteria: Locate reference locals and object fields correctly.
Name at least three non-heap memory consumers.

topics.title: Method frames, references and pass-by-value
topics.description: A call creates a frame and passes argument values.
learningGoals: Explain mutation and reassignment separately.
Trace bounded recursion and its frame lifetimes.
examples: change(List items) adds an entry and then assigns items to a new list.

tasks.title: Record a prediction and runtime assumptions
Run the experiment and keep evidence
Answer the recall questions without notes
Explain a backend failure or design tradeoff

material.explanation: A call creates a frame and passes argument values. For an object argument, the copied value is a reference; two variables can therefore refer to the same mutable object. Reassigning a parameter does not reassign the caller variable, but mutating the shared object can be visible to the caller. Recursion accumulates frames until it returns or exhausts stack capacity. Object reachability and frame lifetime are related, but an object can outlive the method that created it.

workedExample.scenario: change(List items) adds an entry and then assigns items to a new list.
steps: Both caller and callee initially reference the same list, so the add changes that list.
The parameter reassignment changes only the callee local reference.

commonMistakes: Java passes references by value; it does not pass object variables by reference.
guidedExercise: Predict mutation versus reassignment before running the example.
Draw three recursive calls with parameters and return values.
material.independentExercise: Return an object created in a method and explain why it remains usable after the method returns.
recallQuestions: Why does parameter reassignment not change the caller?
What grows during recursion?

acceptanceCriteria: Explain mutation and reassignment separately.
Trace bounded recursion and its frame lifetimes.

material.explanation: Objects have fields and implementation bookkeeping; arrays also carry length information. Alignment and reference representation affect actual footprint, so adding field sizes is not a reliable size calculation. HotSpot commonly uses thread-local allocation buffers for fast allocation, while other allocation paths exist. A reference array stores references, not the referenced objects inline. Inspect layouts with OpenJDK JOL when useful and report the exact VM configuration instead of memorizing one universal header size.

workedExample.scenario: Compare int[1000] with an array of 1000 references to small objects.
steps: Separate the array storage from each referenced object and its overhead.
Inspect representative layouts and report assumptions about reference width and alignment.

commonMistakes: A collection capacity and its logical element count can have different memory costs.
guidedExercise: Estimate a primitive array and an object graph separately.
Compare the estimate with a layout report or heap histogram.
material.independentExercise: Estimate the retained footprint of a map of request records, including keys, entries and referenced payloads.
recallQuestions: Why is shallow size not retained size?
What can change an object layout between JVM runs?

acceptanceCriteria: Account for indirection and array overhead.
Label measurements as implementation-specific.

topics.title: Reachability, GC roots and object lifetime
topics.description: Garbage collection finds objects no longer strongly reachable from roots such as live thread references and class-associated references.
learningGoals: Identify the retaining root path.

material.explanation: Garbage collection finds objects no longer strongly reachable from roots such as live thread references and class-associated references. A cycle alone does not keep objects alive if no root reaches the cycle. Allocating many short-lived objects differs from retaining a growing graph. Collection timing is not a contractual immediate response to setting a variable to null. Weak and soft references have specialized semantics and should not replace an explicit cache size policy.

workedExample.scenario: Two nodes point to each other after the last external reference is removed.
steps: Draw the cycle and show that no root reaches either node.
Contrast it with a static map that still retains one node and therefore the graph.

commonMistakes: Nulling one alias does not remove other strong references; cycles are not automatically leaks.
guidedExercise: Draw roots for a bounded cache and a removed entry.
Trace every remaining reference to the removed value.
material.independentExercise: Explain why a listener registry can keep a service instance alive after a request finishes.
recallQuestions: What makes an object eligible for collection?
How does allocation rate differ from retained memory?

acceptanceCriteria: Identify the retaining root path.
Explain an unreachable cycle correctly.

topics.title: Managed-memory leaks and retention patterns
topics.description: A Java leak often means objects remain reachable longer than intended, not that the collector forgot unreachable memory.
learningGoals: State the retaining owner and lifetime violation.
Compare the post-collection live-set trend under equal load.
examples: A long-lived worker stores each request payload in a static map.

tasks.title: Record a prediction and runtime assumptions
Run the experiment and keep evidence
Answer the recall questions without notes
Explain a backend failure or design tradeoff

material.explanation: A Java leak often means objects remain reachable longer than intended, not that the collector forgot unreachable memory. Common causes include unbounded maps, registries that never unregister listeners, and request data left in ThreadLocal values on reused workers. Rising allocation alone does not establish a leak: compare the live set after comparable collections under a repeatable load. A heap graph can reveal a path to a root; investigate ownership and cleanup before increasing the heap.

workedExample.scenario: A long-lived worker stores each request payload in a static map.
steps: The map retains completed requests, so the post-collection live set grows.
Remove expired entries under an explicit bound and repeat the same load.

commonMistakes: A larger heap can delay a retention failure without fixing its cause.
guidedExercise: List the owner and intended lifetime of each cache or registry.
Use try/finally to remove request-scoped ThreadLocal data on reused workers.
material.independentExercise: Design a bounded cache and a cleanup test that checks retention policy rather than forcing GC as a correctness assertion.
recallQuestions: What evidence distinguishes churn from retention?
Why do reused threads change ThreadLocal lifetime?

acceptanceCriteria: State the retaining owner and lifetime violation.
Compare the post-collection live-set trend under equal load.

topics.title: Garbage collection and allocation pressure
topics.description: Collectors trace reachability and reclaim memory using implementation-specific strategies.
learningGoals: Distinguish allocation rate from live set.
Use workload metrics alongside collection events.
examples: A worker creates temporary parsing objects for every job.

tasks.title: Record a prediction and runtime assumptions
Run the experiment and keep evidence
Answer the recall questions without notes
Explain a backend failure or design tradeoff

material.explanation: Collectors trace reachability and reclaim memory using implementation-specific strategies. Some move live objects, some perform substantial work concurrently, and all require coordination with application execution. Generational designs exploit the tendency of many objects to die young, but Eden and survivor diagrams are not a universal description of every collector. Application allocation rate, retained live set and available CPU shape collection cost. GC can reclaim memory; it cannot close a business transaction or guarantee prompt release of a socket.

workedExample.scenario: A worker creates temporary parsing objects for every job.
steps: Measure jobs per second and bytes allocated over the same interval.
Compare frequent collections with stable live memory against a growing retained set.

commonMistakes: More collections does not alone prove worse performance; compare latency, throughput and CPU.
guidedExercise: Annotate a GC log with allocation bursts and workload phases.
Identify what the selected collector actually reports.
material.independentExercise: Explain why reducing temporary allocations can help a CPU-limited service but might not fix a retained-cache problem.
recallQuestions: Why are young-object diagrams collector-dependent?
Which workload properties determine collection pressure?

acceptanceCriteria: Distinguish allocation rate from live set.
Use workload metrics alongside collection events.

topics.description: Collector choice is a tradeoff among throughput, latency, memory overhead and CPU resources.
learningGoals: Identify the actual collector.

material.explanation: Collector choice is a tradeoff among throughput, latency, memory overhead and CPU resources. G1 uses regions and balances pause goals with reclamation; Parallel emphasizes throughput; Serial is simpler for suitable small workloads; ZGC emphasizes low pauses using concurrent work. Availability and ergonomics depend on the JDK and environment. A pause target is a goal rather than a guaranteed deadline. Identify the current collector first, then compare alternatives under the same representative workload rather than adopting a universal flag bundle.

workedExample.scenario: A batch worker and a latency-sensitive API have different objectives.
steps: Record the active collector from startup or GC diagnostics and establish a baseline.
Compare measured tail latency, CPU and throughput under the same limit before changing collectors.

commonMistakes: A lower GC pause does not automatically mean a faster or cheaper service.
guidedExercise: Write the service objective and its memory/CPU budget.
Choose one collector comparison and list the expected benefit and regression risk.
material.independentExercise: Explain when a throughput-oriented choice might be acceptable despite longer pauses.
recallQuestions: What does a pause target promise?
Why must collector availability be checked on the actual JDK?

acceptanceCriteria: Identify the actual collector.
Compare at least latency, throughput and memory rather than one pause.

topics.description: Some VM operations require threads to reach a state where the VM can safely inspect or modify runtime structures.
learningGoals: Separate pause, queue and blocked time.

material.explanation: Some VM operations require threads to reach a state where the VM can safely inspect or modify runtime structures. A stop-the-world pause is different from concurrent collector work, and reaching a safepoint can contribute its own delay. Request latency can also come from locks, queueing, CPU throttling, network waits or database contention. Correlate timestamps and thread activity before attributing a slow request to GC; averages can conceal rare pauses and queue amplification.

workedExample.scenario: A p99 latency spike occurs with an almost unchanged average.
steps: Align request timestamps with GC and safepoint logs.
If no matching pause exists, inspect blocked threads, queues and external timings.

commonMistakes: Every latency spike is not a garbage collection problem.
guidedExercise: Collect a short local run with -Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags.
Compare events against measured workload latency.
material.independentExercise: Build a timeline showing a lock wait and a collection, then explain which can account for the observed delay.
recallQuestions: How does concurrent GC differ from a global pause?
Why is timestamp correlation necessary?

acceptanceCriteria: Separate pause, queue and blocked time.

topics.title: JIT compilation, warmup and deoptimization
topics.description: HotSpot collects execution information and can compile frequently executed code into optimized machine code.
learningGoals: Label measurement phases.
Explain speculative optimization and deoptimization.
examples: A parsing method runs more quickly after repeated calls.

material.explanation: HotSpot collects execution information and can compile frequently executed code into optimized machine code. Inlining and speculative optimizations can remove work, while changed assumptions can trigger deoptimization. Startup, warmup and steady state are different operating phases. A fast warmed loop does not describe cold server startup, and recompilation activity is not automatically a fault. Compare repeated runs and record the phase being measured rather than timing one first invocation.

workedExample.scenario: A parsing method runs more quickly after repeated calls.
steps: Measure startup and warmed operation separately under equal input.
Inspect compilation activity or JFR evidence and consider caching effects as another explanation.

commonMistakes: Warmup improvement is not proof of one specific optimization without evidence.
guidedExercise: Record throughput over successive fixed workload windows.
Explain which windows represent startup, warmup and steady state.
material.independentExercise: Compare a short-lived command-line task with a long-lived service and explain why optimization priorities differ.
recallQuestions: Why can a method be recompiled?
How can a benchmark accidentally measure only warmup?

acceptanceCriteria: Label measurement phases.
Explain speculative optimization and deoptimization.

material.explanation: HotSpot may prove that an object does not escape the relevant scope and remove its allocation through scalar replacement or other optimizations. This does not mean all non-escaping objects are physically allocated on a stack. Optimizations depend on compilation context and must preserve observable Java behavior. Writing special object-free code without measuring can trade clarity for no gain; first inspect allocation behavior under a representative warmed workload.

workedExample.scenario: A tiny temporary Point is created solely to calculate a sum.
steps: Predict what must remain observable and what a compiler could eliminate.
Measure allocation for a warmed local-use case versus storing the Point in a long-lived collection.

commonMistakes: Escape analysis is not a language guarantee of stack allocation.
guidedExercise: Compare a temporary calculation with an escaping object variant.
Record allocation evidence and the JDK version rather than infer placement from source.

acceptanceCriteria: Separate language guarantees from optimization.

material.explanation: Representation affects allocations and access cost. int[] stores primitive elements while collections of Integer hold references to wrapper objects, with reuse possible in some cases. String storage is implementation-specific and its memory footprint is not simply two bytes times length across all runtimes and text. Concatenation strategies and payload retention also matter. Measure representative data including non-ASCII text; choose a representation based on clarity and workload instead of assuming one fixed object size.

workedExample.scenario: A worker sums numeric IDs from a primitive array and a boxed collection.
steps: Keep equal inputs and arithmetic semantics, including overflow expectations.
Measure allocation and access patterns separately rather than compare unequal preparation work.

commonMistakes: Autoboxing is convenient but its allocation behavior cannot be inferred from syntax alone.
guidedExercise: Identify boxing points in a small loop.

material.independentExercise: Choose a representation for one million IDs and document footprint, access and maintainability tradeoffs.

acceptanceCriteria: Identify boxing and indirection.

topics.title: Visibility, happens-before and atomicity
topics.description: A shared heap does not ensure one thread observes another thread's writes in the required order.
learningGoals: Show a concrete lost-update interleaving.

material.explanation: A shared heap does not ensure one thread observes another thread's writes in the required order. The Java memory model defines happens-before relationships created by mechanisms such as locks, volatile access and thread lifecycle operations. volatile provides ordering and visibility guarantees but does not make count++ an atomic operation. Correct publication and ownership are correctness concerns before performance tuning. A passing stress run is useful evidence, not proof that a data race is safe.

workedExample.scenario: Two threads increment a volatile int counter.
steps: Expand increment into read, add and write
show an interleaving that loses an update.
Replace it with an appropriate atomic operation or locking and state the synchronization guarantee.

commonMistakes: JVM flags and faster hardware cannot repair an incorrectly synchronized algorithm.
guidedExercise: Write a two-thread interleaving on paper.
Choose a visibility example and a separate atomicity example.
material.independentExercise: Explain safe publication of an immutable configuration object and why final fields do not make all referenced mutable data thread-safe.
recallQuestions: Why is volatile increment not atomic?
Which relationship makes a write visible to a reader?

acceptanceCriteria: Show a concrete lost-update interleaving.
Name the happens-before relationship used by the correction.

material.explanation: Platform threads consume operating-system resources and native stack space; large counts can exhaust resources even with a healthy heap. Virtual threads support many blocking tasks with a different implementation and scheduling model; they do not make CPU-bound work unlimited or enlarge database capacity. Their stack storage is not equivalent to reserving one platform-thread stack per virtual thread. Blocking and pinning behavior is version-sensitive, so verify it on the actual JDK rather than repeat older blanket rules about synchronized.

steps: Compare task concurrency with actual downstream concurrency.

topics.description: Heap usage is one part of process memory.
learningGoals: Report heap and process figures separately.

material.explanation: Heap usage is one part of process memory. Native stacks, class metadata, code cache, direct buffers and runtime libraries consume additional memory. Reserved address space, committed memory and resident set size describe different quantities and are not interchangeable. HotSpot Native Memory Tracking reports supported VM allocations but does not account for every allocation made by third-party native code. Use trends and multiple views to locate growth rather than subtract a heap figure from RSS and call the remainder a leak.

steps: Check threads, loaded classes, direct buffers and NMT categories across the same interval.
Compare reserved and committed figures with OS residency while accounting for incomplete native coverage.

guidedExercise: Start a local process with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary.
Run jcmd PID VM.native_memory baseline then jcmd PID VM.native_memory summary.diff after bounded work.
material.independentExercise: Explain how dynamically loaded classes or unreleased direct buffers could change non-heap memory.
recallQuestions: What is reserved versus resident memory?
What does NMT fail to measure completely?

acceptanceCriteria: Report heap and process figures separately.

topics.title: Heap OOM, stack overflow and OS termination
topics.description: Failure classification determines the investigation.
learningGoals: Distinguish four failure classes.
State a specific next observation for each.
examples: A container exits abruptly with no Java exception while heap usage is below -Xmx.

Explain a backend failure or design tradeoff

material.explanation: Failure classification determines the investigation. Java heap exhaustion, metaspace exhaustion and inability to create a native thread can produce different OutOfMemoryError messages. Deep recursion can exhaust stack capacity and produce StackOverflowError. An operating system or container can terminate a process before Java reports any error. Exit code 137 can indicate SIGKILL but is not proof of an OOM kill; correlate events, memory limits and OS evidence. Raising a limit without identifying retention or concurrency can postpone the same failure.

workedExample.scenario: A container exits abruptly with no Java exception while heap usage is below -Xmx.
steps: Inspect termination reason and host/container memory evidence rather than infer from exit code alone.
Budget non-heap usage and compare it with the actual limit.

commonMistakes: Every memory-related failure is not a Java heap leak.
guidedExercise: Build a decision table from symptom, evidence, likely region and next diagnostic.
Use only small bounded child processes if deliberately reproducing errors.
material.independentExercise: Classify three incidents: recursive overflow, unbounded retained records and too many platform threads.
recallQuestions: Can the OS kill a JVM with free heap remaining?
What evidence confirms an OOM kill?

acceptanceCriteria: Distinguish four failure classes.
State a specific next observation for each.

topics.description: Use the least intrusive evidence that can answer the question.
learningGoals: Map symptoms to appropriate tools.
Record collection scope, overhead and artifact handling.
examples: A local worker becomes slow while CPU is low.

tasks.title: Record a prediction and runtime assumptions
Run the experiment and keep evidence
Answer the recall questions without notes
Explain a backend failure or design tradeoff

material.explanation: Use the least intrusive evidence that can answer the question. Thread dumps show states and stacks; repeated samples help distinguish a persistent wait from a momentary snapshot. JFR records time-based runtime events and can expose CPU, allocation and contention patterns. A histogram shows class counts but not full retaining paths; a heap dump enables graph analysis with potentially substantial pause, disk and data exposure costs. Query available commands on the exact target and treat recordings and dumps as potentially sensitive artifacts.

material.explanation: Tune against an explicit latency or throughput objective after measuring a baseline. -Xmx limits Java heap, -Xms sets initial/minimum heap sizing, and -Xss controls thread stack sizing with implementation constraints. None alone limits total process footprint. Percentage-based heap sizing depends on detected memory and ergonomics; inspect effective settings inside the actual container. Leave headroom for native consumers and bursts, and consider CPU quotas and throttling. Change one variable, hold workload constant, report repeatability and keep a rollback criterion.

material.explanation: Backend performance combines algorithmic complexity with representation, cache locality, branch behavior, allocation and workload shape. A primitive array can improve locality compared with traversing separately allocated objects, but the gain is workload- and hardware-dependent. Naive loops can be optimized away or measure setup, warmup or constant folding instead of useful work. Use JMH for an isolated microbenchmark and a representative service workload for user-visible behavior.
